clarity.justification: The method directly tests the hypothesis by fitting “benign-only anomaly models,” evaluating “held-out attack families never in the detector's fit set,” and comparing against Llama-Guard and a supervised classifier using “unseen-attack AUROC, TPR@1%FPR.” The predictions are directional and refutable: MAD must “outperform supervised detectors on unseen attack families,” and feature-co-activation anomalies must be “more discriminative than raw activation anomalies”; equal or worse AUROC/TPR would refute those respective claims, while the 1% FPR operating point adds useful precision. Some implementation-defining choices remain unstated—such as which layers and token positions supply activations, how attack success is labeled, and what magnitude constitutes “substantially outperforms”—so an expert would still need several clarifications.

feasibility.justification: Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Llama-Guard, GCG-style attacks, normalizing flows, Mahalanobis scoring, and SAEs are existing artifacts or methods supported by standard model-hooking, interpretability, and statistical tooling. The hardest step is “anomaly over SAE-feature co-activation patterns”: constructing co-activation statistics is standard, but the graph representation and anomaly-scoring algorithm are not specified, making this a custom-engineering step rather than an impossible magic step. Resources receive partial concrete specification through “Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B,” four named attack families, a classifier trained on “2 attack families,” and “TPR@1%FPR,” although dataset sample sizes, activation layers, and number or provenance of SAEs are absent; importantly, held-out attacks, supervised baselines, the “unusual-benign set,” and the activation-versus-feature ablation provide runnable controls capable of yielding a negative result.
